title: TCP, UDP, ports and reading ss
summary: The transport layer is where 'is it listening?' and 'is it connected?' become answerable. Learn the socket states and the ss output that reveals them.

sections.heading: TCP versus UDP, honestly
sections.html:
TCPUDP
ConnectionThree-way handshake, statefulConnectionless
ReliabilityRetransmission, ordering, flow controlNone — the application decides
Header20+ bytes with sequence/ack numbers8 bytes
Used byHTTP(S), SSH, most databasesDNS, DHCP, QUIC, VoIP, syslog
Failure signatureRefused / timeout / resetSilent loss, application-level timeouts

UDP has no concept of 'refused': a UDP packet to a closed port generates ICMP port-unreachable, but many applications never see it. That is why DNS problems look like timeouts rather than refusals.

sections.heading: Ports and sockets
sections.html:
A TCP connection is identified by the 4-tuple: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. A socket is a kernel object representing one endpoint. A listening socket accepts new connections; an established one is a live connection.

Server ports below 1024 are privileged (need root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE). Ephemeral client ports are typically 32768-60999 on Linux (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range).

sections.heading: ss states that matter
sections.html:
StateMeaningWhere you see it
LISTENWaiting for connectionsServer
SYN-SENTSYN sent, no replyClient — indicates a timeout forming
SYN-RECVSYN received, half-openServer — SYN flood or a broken handshake
ESTABConnection establishedBoth ends
FIN-WAIT-1/2Local side closed, waitingEither — app closed first
TIME-WAITClosed, waiting 2×MSLActive closer — normal, but excessive counts hurt
CLOSE-WAITPeer closed, app has notServer — a leak, the application forgot to close

Two states are genuine red flags when numerous: many SYN-SENT means you are the one timing out; many CLOSE-WAIT means the application is leaking file descriptors; many TIME-WAIT can exhaust ephemeral ports.

sections.heading: The ss commands worth memorising
sections.html:
# listening TCP with process names (the 'is it up?' command)ss -ltnp
# all TCP connections and their statesss -tan
# who is connected to port 5432?ss -tnp '( sport = :5432 )'
# count states - fast summary for a busy serverss -tan | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
# UDP listeners (DNS, DHCP, QUIC)ss -lunp
# what is on a specific port, including which processsudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :80'

Sample output and how to read it:

$ ss -ltnpState   Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN  0      128    0.0.0.0:22            0.0.0.0:*         users:(("sshd",pid=812,fd=3))
LISTEN  0      511    127.0.0.1:5432        0.0.0.0:*         users:(("postgres",pid=1204,fd=7))
LISTEN  0      511    [::]:443               [::]:*            users:(("nginx",pid=1330,fd=8))

Line 2 is the key one: PostgreSQL listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so it is unreachable from the network no matter what the firewall says. Line 3 shows nginx on all IPv6 addresses ([::]), which usually implies all IPv4 too when dual-stack is enabled. Binding address is a security and connectivity decision — this is a real production misconfiguration and a perfect interview example.

sections.heading: netstat and why ss replaced it
sections.html:
netstat is deprecated on Fedora (net-tools is not installed by default). The equivalents:

netstatss
netstat -tlnpss -ltnp
netstat -anss -tan
netstat -rnip route
netstat -iip -s link

Know the mapping for interviews, and know why: ss reads netlink directly, so it is dramatically faster on hosts with tens of thousands of sockets. If a machine has netstat but not ss, it is probably old or an embedded image.

checks.prompt: A service is running and `ss -ltnp` shows it bound to 127.0.0.1:8080. Remote clients get 'connection refused'. Why?
options: The firewall is blocking the port
The service only listens on the loopback address, so it never accepts traffic from the network
checks.explanation: A socket bound to 127.0.0.1 is unreachable from any other host. The kernel has no listener on the external address, so it sends RST — which appears as 'refused', not a timeout.

why_wrong.0: A firewall DROP would produce a timeout, and the binding already explains the symptom.
why_wrong.3: DNS issues produce name-resolution errors, not refusals.

checks.prompt: Which ss output pattern most strongly suggests an application leaking connections?
checks.explanation: CLOSE-WAIT means the peer closed and the local application has not called close(). Persistently growing CLOSE-WAIT is a descriptor leak.

why_wrong.3: TIME-WAIT is normal for the side that closes first.
why_wrong.1: SYN-RECV suggests a handshake not completing, commonly a SYN flood.

checks.prompt: A developer says 'the API is running but nobody can reach it'. What do you check, in order, and what would each result mean?

checklist.text: Confirm a listener exists and on which address/port (ss -ltnp).
Check the local firewall and any cloud security group/ACL.
Test from the client: refusal means RST (no listener or reject rule), timeout means drop.
Confirm routing and that the client is using the right address (DNS may point elsewhere).
Check the service's own logs for bind errors or startup failures.

checks.reference: First prove a listener exists and note its address: ss -ltnp. If it is bound to 127.0.0.1, that alone explains the failure. If it is on 0.0.0.0 or a specific external address, test from the client and read the error precisely: immediate refusal means an RST reached you (listener absent on that address, or a reject rule); a hang means packets are dropped (firewall, security group, wrong route). Check the service logs for bind errors and confirm the client is connecting to the address DNS actually returns. Order matters because each step eliminates a whole class of cause.

connect.title: DNS
connect.text: Resolution gets you an address; the socket decides whether anything answers on that address and port.

connect.title: Firewalls
connect.text: DROP gives timeout, REJECT gives refusal — the difference is a firewall policy signal.

connect.title: Process management
connect.text: ss -p links a port to a PID, which is how you find the process that owns the socket.

interview.q: What is the difference between connection refused and connection timed out?
interview.a: Refused means a TCP RST came back — the host is reachable and nothing is listening (or a reject rule fired). Timed out means no response at all — a DROP rule, a dead host, or a black-holed route. Refusal is fast and specific; timeout is silent.

interview.q: How do you find which process listens on a port?
interview.a: sudo ss -ltnp with a filter for the port, which shows the PID and process name. lsof -i :port and fuser also work. If the process is in another namespace or container, you need to run the tool inside that namespace.
